extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry, literary critics, and readers learning practical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading, evaluating, and teaching poetry with attention to tone, the relation of sense and feeling, metaphor, and poetic form (rhythm). Emphasises diagnostic criteria for faults and virtues in poems and for critical method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone / relation of writer to reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the secrets of “style” are matters of tone, of the perfect recognition of the writer’s relation to the reader in view of what is being said and their joint feelings about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the writer accommodates his feelings to the discriminating attention of his audience (example: Gray). Faults of tone include 'overdoing' or taking refuge in elliptic hinting; these are not mere surface blemishes but may indicate deep disorder. Assess whether tone reflects a correct sense of proportion and appropriate manners for the intended reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remembering / respecting the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Eighteenth-century writers rarely forget the reader; good tone does not require constant flattery but occasions when the reader is ignored must be exciting enough to justify the poet’s rapt oblivion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether instances of ignoring or flattering the reader are justified by the content; note that neglecting the reader (condescension, over-insistence) can ruin otherwise valuable poetry. Distinguish deliberate rhetorical address from mere neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overstressing and inappropriate discovery-tone
rubrics_metrics.description: When a commonplace is delivered with an air appropriate to a fresh discovery or a revelation, we can properly grow suspicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for 'overdoing'—presenting familiar sentiment as if it were novel; this often insults the reader and may indicate the author's rank or clumsiness. Good manners require proportionate emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sound (sensuous aspect) of words influences feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The sound of a word has plainly much to do with the feeling it evokes, above all when it occurs in the organised context of a passage of verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating feeling, take account of phonetic and sensuous properties (sound, rhythm, dance-movement of speech organs) as one of the causes of the feeling, alongside history, semantics, usual contexts, and special context in the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type I — feeling generated by sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling evoked is the result of apprehending the sense; sense and feeling form an indissoluble whole (examples: 'miraculous', 'sorcery').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify words whose sense naturally and inevitably produces a particular feeling; such words seldom vary in emotional effect across contexts. Treat these as lexical items whose meaning carries the feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type II — sense derived from feeling (projectile/aesthetic adjectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word first expresses a feeling, and such sense as it conveys is derived from the feeling (example: 'gorgeous'—a 'projectile' adjective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise projectile adjectives and aesthetic terms that project feeling onto objects; analysis should consider how these words shape sense by virtue of their emotive force and customary uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type III — feeling determined by context (malleable words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Here sense and feeling are less closely knit: the feeling of a word arises from the influence of the rest of the poem rather than inevitably from its sense (example: 'sprawling').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether context 'pulls' a word into the poem or whether the word 'resists' and disturbs the poem's tone. Words of malleable feeling may take on varying emotions depending on collocation; evaluate the contextual transactions that produce that feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical fit and resistance (word vs. whole poem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the pull exerted by the context sufficient to overcome the normal separate feeling of the questionable word? Or does the word resist, stay outside, or wrench the rest of the poem into crudity or confusion?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a poet’s power or discretion by whether he 'triumphs over the resistances of words' (Shakespeare example). Consider whether a word fits harmoniously or creates discord, and whether discord is intentional and effective or merely clumsy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual control of feeling (direct and via sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of the rest of the poem upon the single word or phrase is exerted in two ways—directly between feelings and indirectly through sense (transactions between parts of the sense in the whole passage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a line or phrase, consider both emotional interplay with existing feelings in the reader’s mind and logical/semantic relations within the passage that alter the word’s feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantaneity of apprehension vs. analytic understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: A definite and relevant feeling can be aroused at once; feeling that is quite pertinent seems often to precede any clear grasping of the sense. Apprehension may be instantaneous while discursive analysis is slow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that immediate responses are real and important, but guard against undervaluing analytic work; recognise three causes (intuitive grasp vs later analysis, dissociation in reading, compression of poetic language). Use both immediate response and careful analysis in judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of paraphrase — separate paraphrases for sense and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a paraphrase or gloss for any poem worth reading is a delicate exercise; a single paraphrase will rarely indicate more than a single partial aspect of a poem—one paraphrase for sense and another to suggest feeling may be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware the danger that logical expansion substitutes a 'bad piece of prose' for the poem. Teachers and readers should use paraphrase cautiously; exercise in analysis must avoid forcing the poem into prose meanings that misrepresent its feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and methods for describing feelings (vocabulary and metaphors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling is harder to analyse than sense; we rely on introspection, aesthetic adjectives, emotive metaphors, qualifying words, and the dictionary as a repository of distinctions about feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish emotive from sense metaphors; note compatibilities and incompatibilities among aesthetic adjectives (e.g., pretty vs sublime). Use language resources carefully and seek metaphors that present rather than merely name feelings. Encourage study of metaphor to improve critical description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet’s craft: controlling feeling through metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet’s task is constantly (though not only) that of finding ways and means of controlling feeling through metaphor; he must be expert in presenting feeling as well as describing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a poet, attend to originality and effectiveness of metaphor in both presenting feelings (evoking them) and describing them; distinguish analytic ability to explain metaphors from creative power to invent them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of introspection and the role of linguistic records
rubrics_metrics.description: Introspection about feelings is untrustworthy; much knowledge about feelings is 'lying dormant in the dictionary'—language records distinctions we have not yet systematised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dictionaries and historical/semantic study to uncover subtle distinctions of feeling; combine psychological insight with literary analysis rather than relying solely on introspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and poetic form — irregularity vs arrangement of departures
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion that regularity is the merit of verse is misleading; the best verses are frequently irregular. Metrical excellence lies in an arrangement of departures from and returns to a pattern rather than strict conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging poetic rhythm, avoid crude rule-based scansion as the sole test. Prefer judgments that account for organised variation, interaction of rhythm with meaning, and movement of words in verse. Train ears and analytical understanding together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of form and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Half perhaps of the feeling that poetry carries comes through its form (and through the interaction of form and content); rhythm is not simply a character of sounds apart from their effects in the mind of the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate form (rhythm, movement, lineation) in its relation to sense and feeling: assess how formal features contribute to emotional effect and meaning rather than treating them as independent qualities.
